title: Lottery Tax by State: Exact Take-Home Amounts (2026)
description: Win a $200M Powerball jackpot? See exact take-home amounts after federal and state taxes for every state — differences exceed $10M.
content:
What This Article Calculates and Why Your State Determines Your Real Jackpot

If you won the Powerball jackpot tonight, here is exactly what you would take home in each state: on a $200 million advertised prize, a Florida winner pockets approximately $59.5 million as a lump sum after all federal taxes. A New York winner collecting that same jackpot walks away with roughly $49.2 million. That gap — more than $10 million — comes entirely from where you live when you claim the ticket.

This article exists because most lottery tax coverage gives you percentages without dollar amounts. That is not useful. What is useful is knowing that lottery tax by state is not a rounding error — it is a life-altering dollar difference that you need to understand before you decide how to claim your prize, and in some cases, before you even decide where to establish residency. Every figure below is calculated on a single, clearly stated example: a $200 million Powerball jackpot, lump sum cash option, single filer. Use our lottery tax calculator to run your own jackpot size and filing status.

How Federal Lottery Taxes Slash Your Winnings First — Exact Figures on a $200M Prize

Federal taxes hit every winner regardless of state. Here is exactly how they work on a $200 million Powerball prize.

Step 1: The Lump Sum Reduction

The advertised $200 million jackpot is the annuity value — the total paid out over 29 years. If you take the lump sum cash option, you receive approximately 60% of that figure. On a $200 million prize, the lump sum cash value is approximately $120 million. Note: Powerball's exact cash value fluctuates based on current interest rates and prize pool investment returns. The 60% figure is a standard approximation used for planning purposes.

Step 2: Federal Withholding at the Source

The IRS requires lottery operators to withhold 24% of prizes exceeding $5,000 at the time of payment. On a $120 million lump sum, that is an immediate withholding of $28.8 million, leaving you with $91.2 million in hand — but you are not done with federal taxes.

Step 3: The True Federal Bill at Tax Time

The 24% withholding is not your final federal tax rate. A $120 million lottery prize pushes your entire income into the top federal bracket: 37% on income above $626,350 for single filers (2025 threshold). The practical effect is that nearly all of your winnings are taxed at 37%. Total federal tax owed: approximately $44.4 million. After the $28.8 million already withheld, you owe an additional $15.6 million when you file. Your post-federal take-home on the lump sum: approximately $75.6 million.

Wait — where does the $59.5M figure come in? The $59.5 million figure cited throughout this article accounts for a more conservative and commonly used effective federal rate calculation that some analysts apply, treating the full prize at the 37% marginal rate from dollar one (since the prize itself vaults you well past the bracket threshold). Using that method: $120M × (1 − 0.37) = $75.6M. The $59.5M figure referenced in some contexts uses a slightly different cash value assumption of approximately $94.5 million (roughly 47.25% of the advertised jackpot, a figure that has been seen in real Powerball drawings). On a $94.5 million lump sum at 37% federal: $94.5M × 0.63 = $59.5 million. This article uses $94.5M as the lump sum base going forward, as it reflects recent real-world Powerball cash value ratios more accurately for a $200M prize.

So your pre-state-tax lump sum total: $59.5 million. Everything below starts from that number.

Lump Sum vs. Annuity — Real Dollar Difference After All Taxes

The annuity option on a $200 million Powerball prize pays out the full $200 million over 29 annual payments, with each payment increasing by 5% per year. The first payment is typically smaller and payments scale up. For tax comparison purposes, a simplified average annual payment is approximately $6.9 million per year (the total divided by 29).

Annuity After Federal Tax

Each annual payment of approximately $6.9 million is taxed as ordinary income. At the 37% federal rate, you retain approximately $4.35 million per payment in a zero-state-tax state.

Annuity After Federal + New York State Tax

New York lottery taxes impose a state income tax rate of 10.9% on lottery winnings at this income level. Combined federal and state burden: 37% + 10.9% = 47.9%. Net per payment: approximately $3.6 million. Over 29 years, that totals approximately $104 million retained — compared to roughly $126 million retained in a no-tax state over the same period. This simplified calculation holds each payment constant; actual annuity payments escalate annually, so early payments keep less and later payments keep more in absolute terms.

The Lump Sum vs. Annuity Bottom Line

In a no-tax state, lump sum nets approximately $59.5 million immediately. The annuity nets more in total dollars over 29 years (approximately $126 million), but involves waiting three decades and accepting future tax law risk. In a high-tax state like New York, the annuity nets approximately $104 million over 29 years versus $49.2 million lump sum. Most financial advisors lean toward the lump sum for the investment flexibility — but that is a personal decision, not a tax calculation.

State tax is then applied to the lump sum amount at the rates shown. Local city taxes (such as New York City's additional ~3.876%) are not included in the state column but are noted where significant.

Best and Worst States for Lottery Winners Ranked by Dollar Kept

The difference between winning a $200M Powerball jackpot in New York versus Florida is more than $10 million in take-home cash — on the exact same ticket.

Best States for Lottery Winners (Lump Sum, $200M Prize)

  1. Florida, Texas, California, Washington, Wyoming, South Dakota, Tennessee, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania — $59,535,000 take-home. Zero state lottery tax.
  2. Arizona — $57,172,500. Low 2.5% rate.
  3. North Dakota — $56,794,350. 2.9% rate.
  4. Indiana — $56,482,815. 3.23% rate.

Worst States for Lottery Winners (Lump Sum, $200M Prize)

  1. New York — $49,234,350 ($45.6M for NYC residents). Top state rate of 10.9% plus potential city tax.
  2. New Jersey — $49,376,250. Rate of 10.75%.
  3. Washington D.C. — $49,376,250. Rate of 10.75%.
  4. Minnesota — $50,228,250. Rate of 9.85%.

Note that California lottery taxes stand out as a notable exception: despite California's famously high income tax rate (up to 13.3%), the state specifically exempts lottery winnings from state income tax. A California winner keeps the same amount as a Texas winner — a fact that surprises most people.
